summary: Reorganizes the names of already-allocated TLV types and type extensions in the MANET parameters registries from RFC 5444 so the names are used appropriately. It changes nothing in how protocols behave. It also updates the Expert Review guidelines so future names are chosen consistently.

plainLanguage.summary: Some labels in a big filing cabinet had confusing names. This renames them to be tidy without moving anything inside.

questions: what is tlv naming in manet
how are manet tlv types named in the iana registry
what is a tlv type extension
how are manet tlv registries named
subtitle: A pure naming cleanup of the MANET TLV registries so type extensions can be allocated without misleading names.

tldr.problem: In the MANET packet format, many TLV types were named after just their first type extension (such as LINK_STATUS), which made the other 255 type extensions look unavailable or oddly named.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC moves such names from the TLV type to the full type (type plus extension 0), renames the IANA registries to Type XX form, and updates the Expert Review guidelines for future allocations.
tldr.outcome: Nothing about protocol behavior changes; only names in documents and IANA registries do. It updates RFC 5444 and has itself been updated by RFC 7722.

today: RFC 7631 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5444 and has itself been updated by RFC 7722. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Naming Problem
sections.content:
RFC 5444 defines a generalized packet and message format for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs), with TLVs (type-length-value structures) at the packet, message and address block levels. IANA records them in the "Packet TLV Types", "Message TLV Types" and "Address Block TLV Types" subregistries.

A TLV has a one-octet type and a one-octet type extension, which together form a two-octet full type. The extension may be omitted when it is zero, but it is still zero. Each TLV type has its own IANA registry of type extensions.

This document identifies two styles of allocation. In the first, allocating the type defines all its extensions, as with LINK_METRIC, so naming the type is fine. In the second, more common style, only extension 0 (and possibly 1) was defined, as with LINK_STATUS in RFC 6130. Naming the whole type after one extension leaves extensions 1 to 255 either unusable or misleadingly named.
sections.plainLanguage: Some drawers in the cabinet were labelled with the name of just the first folder inside. That made it look like the whole drawer was only for that one thing.

sections.title: The Fix: Name the Full Type
sections.content:
For the second style, the name now attaches to the full type rather than the TLV type. For example, LINK_STATUS becomes the name of the full type made of TLV type 3 and extension 0, and stops being the name of type 3. Because it is not clear what other TLVs might use the other extensions, the type itself is left unnamed and identified by number.

The RFC states plainly that nothing in it changes the operation of any protocol. The naming is already used in effect in RFC 6130 and RFC 7181, the main users of allocated TLVs. All currently allocated TLVs from RFC 5497, RFC 6130, RFC 6621, RFC 7181 and RFC 7182 are listed in the IANA section, with updates or an indication of no change, and the only changes are of naming.
sections.plainLanguage: Now the label goes on the folder, not the drawer. The drawer gets just a number, so other folders can be added later.

sections.title: New Expert Review Guidelines
sections.content:
The Expert Review guidelines from RFC 5444 are extended for the three TLV type registries. If a requested TLV type defines all its type extensions at once, a common name SHOULD be assigned. This case is unchanged and covers ICV, TIMESTAMP and LINK_METRIC, plus the HELLO Message-Type-specific TLVs of RFC 6621.

Otherwise a common name SHOULD NOT be given to the type. It is RECOMMENDED instead that:

  • the description of the type be "Defined by Type Extension";
  • the extension registry be named "Type XX Packet TLV Type Extensions", "Type XX Message TLV Type Extensions" or "Type XX Address Block TLV Type Extensions", with XX the numeric type;
  • a new extension normally takes the next consecutive number, unless there are reasons to the contrary, such as keeping packet, message and address block TLVs in correspondence or reserving extension zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule for new labels: if a TLV uses the whole drawer, name the drawer. If not, just number the drawer and name each folder.

sections.title: What Changed in the Registries
sections.content:
The long second half of the IANA section walks through each registry. Registries such as "INTERVAL_TIME Message Type Extensions" are renamed "Type 0 Message TLV Type Extensions", "VALIDITY_TIME" becomes Type 1, "MPR_WILLING" becomes Type 7 and "CONT_SEQ_NUM" becomes Type 8. In the Message TLV Types table, types 0, 1, 7 and 8 become "Defined by Type Extension", while types 5 and 6 stay ICV and TIMESTAMP.

For address blocks, types 0 to 4 and 8 to 10 become "Defined by Type Extension", types 5 and 6 stay ICV and TIMESTAMP, and type 7 stays LINK_METRIC. The old LOCAL_IF, LINK_STATUS, OTHER_NEIGHB, MPR, NBR_ADDR_TYPE and GATEWAY names move to extension 0 of types 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 and 10. Several other registries are listed as unchanged, and the Packet TLV Types registry is unchanged.

The document also corrects a small omission: it adds reservations for Experimental Use, left out of RFC 7181, to the last three tables (extensions 224 to 255 for types 8, 9 and 10).
sections.plainLanguage: The rest of the document goes label by label through the cabinet and says which ones were moved from the drawer to the first folder.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it has no security considerations. Its reasoning is that it is concerned only with how entities are named, and those names are used only in documents like this one and in IANA registries.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the names on labels does not change what is inside the cabinet, so there is nothing new to guard.
